These examples show how to apply M3 to simple-span and complex-span tasks.
In simple span, M3 measures item memory and binding memory; in complex span,
it adds a filtering parameter.

## Setup


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(bmm)
library(brms)
library(tidyverse)
library(tidybayes)
library(here)

source(here("_common.R"))  # shared workshop colors + ggplot theme
```
:::


## Data

The data come from two experiments by Oberauer (2019). Participants studied
words in boxes and then selected the word associated with a probed position.
There were 40 participants: 20 studied new words on every trial (`openset`),
and 20 studied words drawn repeatedly from a small set (`closedset`). Each
participant completed four set-size conditions (2, 4, 6, and 8 items).
Responses fall into three categories: the correct item, another studied
item, or a non-presented lure. The data contain aggregated response counts;
column definitions and data preparation are documented in the
[codebook](../data/README.md).


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
dat_simple <- read.csv(here("data", "m3_simple_span.csv"))
dat_simple$exp <- factor(dat_simple$exp, levels = c("openset", "closedset"))
dat_simple$ss_fac <- factor(dat_simple$ss_fac, levels = c(2, 4, 6, 8))
glimpse(dat_simple)
```

The response-count columns `corr`, `other`, and `npl` sum to 23 in each row.
The `n_*` columns give the number of available test options in each category;
zero means that category was absent from the options.

## Specify: activation and response categories

The simple-span M3 measures memory strength along two dimensions: item
memory ($a$), memory for the studied items, and binding memory ($c$), memory
for the associations between items and their positions (Oberauer &
Lewandowsky, 2019). The table shows how these parameters contribute to each
response category's activation, with baseline activation fixed at zero for
the softmax model.

| Response category | Response-count column | Activation per option | Option-count column |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Correct item | `corr` | $a + c$ | `n_corr` |
| Other studied item | `other` | $a$ | `n_other` |
| Not-presented lure | `npl` | $0$ | `n_npl` |

In `m3()`, `resp_cats` names the response-count columns and `num_options`
names the corresponding option-count columns. **Both vectors must follow
the table's order: correct, other studied items, then not-presented lures.**

`version = "ss"` supplies these simple-span activation functions.
The choice rule converts activation into response probabilities, taking the
number of available options in each category into account. Here,
`choice_rule = "softmax"` uses exponentiated activation values as weights,
which are normalized across the available response options.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
model_simple <- m3(
  resp_cats = c("corr", "other", "npl"),
  num_options = c("n_corr", "n_other", "n_npl"),
  version = "ss",
  choice_rule = "softmax"
)
model_simple
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
m3(resp_cats = c("corr", "other", "npl"),    num_options = c("n_corr", "n_other", "n_npl"),    choice_rule = "softmax",    version = "ss") 
Parameters: b, c, a 
Fixed:      b = 0 
Use parameters() for more details.
```


:::
:::


`bmf()` supplies one regression formula per cognitive parameter. Specify how
the parameters vary across experiments, set sizes, and participants:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
formula_simple <- bmf(
  c ~ 0 + exp:ss_fac + (1 + ss_fac | gr(id, by = exp)),
  a ~ 0 + exp:ss_fac + (1 + ss_fac | gr(id, by = exp))
)
formula_simple
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
c ~ 0 + exp:ss_fac + (1 + ss_fac | gr(id, by = exp))
a ~ 0 + exp:ss_fac + (1 + ss_fac | gr(id, by = exp))
```


:::
:::


Here, `0 + exp:ss_fac` estimates a separate $a$ and $c$ for each experiment × set
size cell.

`(1 + ss_fac | gr(id, by = exp))` allows participants to differ in their
overall activation and set-size effects, with separate participant-effect
distributions for the two experiments.

Check that `Rhat` is near 1 (ideally below 1.01) and that there are no
divergent transitions. Bulk and tail ESS describe the effective sample sizes
for posterior summaries. `nuts_params()` provides sampler diagnostics;
use it to count divergent transitions:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
nuts <- nuts_params(fit_simple)
sum(nuts$Value[nuts$Parameter == "divergent__"])
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0
```


:::
:::


The cached simple-span fit has no divergent transitions, and all Rhat values
are below 1.01.

### Optional: re-fit the model yourself

Re-fit the simple-span model if needed. This optional step requires the
Stan toolchain (`Install_Packages.R`, Part 2) and overwrites the cached fit.
`bmm()` combines the model, formulas, and data. `file_refit = "always"`
forces a new fit even when a cached file exists.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
fit_simple <- bmm(
  formula = formula_simple,
  model = model_simple,
  data = dat_simple,
  prior = c(
    prior(normal(3, 1), class = "b", nlpar = "a"),
    prior(normal(3, 1), class = "b", nlpar = "c")
  ),
  chains = 4, cores = 4, iter = 4000, warmup = 2000,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99),
  sample_prior = "yes", backend = "cmdstanr", seed = 2026,
  file = here("models", "m3_simple"), file_refit = "always"
)
```
:::


The [fitting script](../models/fit_m3.R) contains both fits. To re-fit a model
with that script, change its `file_refit` setting from `"never"` to `"always"`.

## Evaluate: model-implied response proportions

`posterior_epred()` gives expected counts in each response category.
Use these to compare observed and predicted response proportions:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Prepare observed and predicted counts.
observed_counts <- dat_simple |> select(id, exp, setsize, corr, other, npl)

set.seed(2026)
expected_counts <- posterior_epred(fit_simple, ndraws = 200)
predicted_counts <- dat_simple |> select(id, exp, setsize)
# Average over draws, retaining data rows and response categories.
predicted_counts[c("corr", "other", "npl")] <- apply(expected_counts, c(2, 3), mean)

# Calculate participant proportions and summarise across participants.
pp_data <- bind_rows(
  Observed = observed_counts,
  Predicted = predicted_counts,
  .id = "source"
) |>
  summarise(
    corr = sum(corr),
    other = sum(other),
    npl = sum(npl),
    .by = c(source, id, exp, setsize)
  ) |>
  mutate(total = corr + other + npl) |>
  pivot_longer(
    c(corr, other, npl),
    names_to = "category",
    values_to = "count"
  ) |>
  mutate(proportion = count / total) |>
  summarise(
    se = sd(proportion) / sqrt(n()),
    proportion = mean(proportion),
    .by = c(source, exp, setsize, category)
  )

pp_data$category <- factor(
  pp_data$category,
  levels = c("corr", "other", "npl"),
  labels = c("Correct", "Other items", "NPL")
)
```
:::


Averaging 200 posterior draws produces one set of predictions per data row.
The code then combines observed and predicted counts, calculates each
participant's response proportions, and summarises their means and
standard errors (SE).


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Keep the y-axis identical across experiments within each category column.
pp_limits <- pp_data |>
  summarise(ymin = min(pmax(0, proportion - se)),
            ymax = max(pmin(1, proportion + se)), .by = category) |>
```

## Extension: complex span

Li, Frischkorn, and Oberauer (2026), Experiment 1, added distractor processing
to the memory task. Participants studied three target images while making
size judgments. Targets were cued before processing (**pre-cue**) or after
processing (**retro-cue**); a **control** condition contained no distractors.
The tutorial preparation retains 45 participants, with one row per participant
× condition. See the [codebook](../data/README.md) for exclusions and column definitions.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
dat_complex <- read.csv(here("data", "m3_complex_span.csv"))
dat_complex$condition <- factor(dat_complex$condition,
                                levels = c("control", "pre", "retro"))
head(dat_complex, 3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

1           1   control   41    18     0     0   1      1       2       0
2           1       pre   31    17     4     6   1      1       2       1
3           1     retro   34    15     5     4   1      1       2       1
  n_disto n_npl
1       0     9
2       2     6
3       2     6
```

:::


### Specify the additional response categories

The complex-span model adds a filtering parameter $f$, which scales
distractor activation relative to target activation: $f = 0$
means no activation beyond baseline, while $f = 1$ means distractors receive
the same activation as targets. Thus, lower $f$ indicates stronger filtering.
It is an activation multiplier, not the proportion of distractors remembered
or filtered out. The activation formulas now include five response categories:

| Response category | Count column | Softmax activation | Option-count column |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Correct item | `corr` | $a+c$ | `n_corr` |
| Distractor paired with the tested target | `distc` | $f(a+c)$ | `n_distc` |
| Other target item | `other` | $a$ | `n_other` |
| Other distractor | `disto` | $fa$ | `n_disto` |
| Not-presented lure | `npl` | $0$ | `n_npl` |

`version = "cs"` supplies the complex-span activation functions. Supply the
response and option-count columns in the category order shown above.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
model_complex <- m3(
  resp_cats = c("corr", "distc", "other", "disto", "npl"),
  num_options = c("n_corr", "n_distc", "n_other", "n_disto", "n_npl"),
  version = "cs", choice_rule = "softmax"
)
```
:::


Specify how the parameters vary across conditions and participants:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
formula_complex <- bmf(
  c ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition || participant),
  a ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition || participant),
  f ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition || participant)
)
```
:::


The formulas estimate condition-specific parameters and uncorrelated
participant deviations. Control has no distractors, so $f$ cannot be
estimated in that condition and is fixed in the fitting script.

### Check the five response categories

Calculate the model-implied response counts:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(2026)
expected_counts_complex <- posterior_epred(fit_complex, ndraws = 200)
pred_complex <- apply(expected_counts_complex, c(2, 3), mean)
colnames(pred_complex) <- c("corr", "distc", "other", "disto", "npl")
```
:::


The predictions are averaged over 200 posterior draws and retain the
model's response-category order.

Summarise observed and predicted response proportions:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pp_complex <- bind_rows(
  Observed = dat_complex |>
    select(participant, condition, corr, distc, other, disto, npl),
  Predicted = bind_cols(dat_complex |> select(participant, condition),
                        as_tibble(pred_complex)),
  .id = "source"
) |>
  mutate(total = corr + distc + other + disto + npl) |>
  pivot_longer(c(corr, distc, other, disto, npl),
               names_to = "category", values_to = "count") |>
  mutate(proportion = count / total,
         category = factor(category, levels = c("corr", "other", "distc", "disto", "npl"),
                           labels = c("Correct", "Other items", "Paired distractor",
                                      "Other distractors", "NPL"))) |>
  summarise(se = sd(proportion) / sqrt(n()), proportion = mean(proportion),
            .by = c(source, condition, category))
```
:::


The participant summaries use the same mean and SE calculations as for
simple span.

### Read activation and filtering estimates

`plogis()` transforms logit-scale values to the 0–1 scale.
Summarise the activation and filtering estimates:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
complex_parameters <- as.data.frame(fit_complex) |>
  select(matches("^b_[acf]_condition")) |>
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = c("parameter", "condition"),
    names_pattern = "^b_([acf])_condition(control|pre|retro)$",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  filter(!(parameter == "f" & condition == "control")) |>
  mutate(
    value = if_else(parameter == "f", plogis(value), value),
    parameter = factor(parameter, levels = c("a", "c", "f")),
    condition = factor(condition, levels = c("control", "pre", "retro"))
  ) |>
  summarise(median_qi(value), .by = c(parameter, condition))
complex_parameters |>
  select(parameter, condition, median = y, lower = ymin, upper = ymax)
```
